## Worldview
Baghdad, the City of Peace, is not yet seventy years old and is the largest city west of China, with several hundred thousand people (estimates vary widely). It is still repairing the damage of the siege of 812–813, when al-Ma'mun's armies took it from his brother al-Amin. Al-Ma'mun has ruled from here since 819 and spends these years on campaign against Byzantium. God is one and the Quran is His word; whether that word is created or eternal is the question the caliph has made a matter of state. He favours the rational theologians of the Mu'tazila against the traditionists, and in 833 he will make every judge swear to it. Learning is prized, and patrons pay for it. Greek books in philosophy, medicine, mathematics and astronomy are being turned into Arabic, mostly through Syriac and mostly by Christian scholars, beside Persian and Indian works. Aristotle, Galen, Euclid and Ptolemy are authorities to be understood and reconciled, not tested; nobody yet expects an experiment to overrule them. Astrology is a learned profession. Medicine is Galenic and in the hands of Nestorian Christian physicians. Paper is made in the city and is replacing papyrus in the offices, but every book is copied by hand. Indian numerals with a sign for zero are known to a few astronomers and are not yet used by clerks. Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians live under protection and pay the poll tax. Slavery is everywhere, from household servants and singing girls to the Turkish soldiers that the caliph's brother is buying.

## People
- **Abd Allah al-Ma'mun**: Abbasid caliph since 813, in Baghdad since 819; patron of the translations and the observatories. Knows: Mu'tazilite theology and disputation, astronomy and astrology at a patron's level, the army and the Byzantine frontier. — Born 786, son of Harun al-Rashid and a Persian concubine. Away on campaign each summer from 830 (Cilicia, Cappadocia) and in Damascus and Egypt in 831–832. Dies of a fever on campaign near Tarsus on 7 August 833, months after ordering the Mihna.
- **Abu Ishaq Muhammad al-Mu'tasim**: the caliph's half-brother, commander, his successor in 833. Knows: soldiering; builds a private army of Turkish slave-soldiers (ghilman) bought in Samarkand and Baghdad. — Barely literate by the chroniclers' account, practical, respected by the troops. Moves the court to Samarra in 836. His son Ahmad will be al-Kindi's pupil.
- **al-Abbas ibn al-Ma'mun**: the caliph's son and frontier commander. Knows: the Jazira and the Byzantine frontier forts. — Takes Tyana in 831; in May 833 starts building a fortress base there. Passed over for the succession; dies in prison in 838 after a plot against al-Mu'tasim.
- **Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi**: mathematician, astronomer and geographer in the caliph's service. Knows: al-Jabr wa'l-muqabala (completion and balancing), solving quadratics in words with geometric proof; reckoning with the nine Indian digits and zero; an astronomical table on the Sindhind model; a geography revising Ptolemy's coordinates. — Born c. 780, origin in Khwarazm (the nisba may only be ancestral). Associated with the House of Wisdom; reported present at the Shammasiyya solstice observations of 828. Dies c. 850. His algebra was dedicated to al-Ma'mun and is new; how far clerks use it is unknown. His Picture of the Earth (geography) is usually dated to these years, finished by about 833.
- **Abu Yusuf Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi**: young Arab aristocrat and scholar at court, later 'the philosopher of the Arabs'. Knows: what the translators bring him, Aristotle, Euclid, Ptolemy, Indian numerals; will write on optics, music, medicine dosage, cryptanalysis, perfumes and swords. — Born c. 800 in Kufa or Basra to a family of the Kinda tribe; his father governed Kufa. Under al-Ma'mun he is beginning; his main work falls under al-Mu'tasim and al-Wathiq. Directs translators rather than translating himself.
- **Muhammad, Ahmad and al-Hasan ibn Musa ibn Shakir (the Banu Musa)**: three brothers, sons of a former highwayman turned astronomer, raised at court as wards of al-Ma'mun. Knows: geometry, astronomy, mechanics; later famous for the Book of Ingenious Devices (c. 850) and for hiring translators with their own money. — Young in 830 (Muhammad born before 803), under the guardianship of Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Mus'abi. Ahmad is the mechanician, al-Hasan the geometer, Muhammad the astronomer and later the politician. Later sources credit them with a share in the degree measurement; doubtful at their age.
- **Yuhanna ibn Masawayh**: Nestorian Christian physician to the caliph, teacher of medicine. Knows: Galenic medicine, drugs and aromatics, eye disease (writes the first Arabic book on ophthalmology, Daghal al-'ayn); later dissects apes for anatomy. — Born c. 777, son of a pharmacist from Gondeshapur. Sharp-tongued; famously sends away a student who asked too many questions, Hunayn. Dies in Samarra in 857.
- **Hunayn ibn Ishaq**: young Christian (Ibadi) scholar from al-Hira, translator in the making. Knows: Syriac, Arabic, increasingly Greek; Galen. — Born 808 or 809, son of a pharmacist. After his dismissal by Ibn Masawayh he goes abroad (Byzantine lands or Alexandria) to learn Greek; when exactly he returns is uncertain, probably by the late 820s or early 830s. Works first for physicians and for the Banu Musa; his great Galen translations come in the 840s to 870s.
- **Bukhtishu ibn Jibril**: court physician, head of the richest Christian medical family. Knows: Gondeshapur medicine, court politics. — His father Jibril, physician to Harun and al-Ma'mun, died c. 827. Bukhtishu serves the caliphs on and off until his death in 870.
- **Salmawayh ibn Bunan**: Nestorian Christian physician to al-Ma'mun, then to al-Mu'tasim. Knows: Galenic clinical medicine. — Presumably in the caliph's train on campaign. Al-Mu'tasim calls him father and prays over his grave when he dies in 840.
- **Sahl ibn Harun**: secretary, writer and head of the caliph's library (Khizanat al-Hikma). Knows: Persian court literature and adab; the library's holdings. — Persian by origin; with a colleague, Salm, he runs the palace library that later sources call the Bayt al-Hikma. Famous for an essay praising thrift. Usually said to die in AH 215 (830), so meet him early.
- **al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn Matar**: translator of Greek mathematics. Knows: Euclid's Elements (he made one version for Harun and an improved one for al-Ma'mun) and the Almagest, translated through Syriac about 827–829. — Reachable in Baghdad; little else is known of his life.
- **Yahya ibn Abi Mansur**: Persian astronomer of a Zoroastrian family (the Banu al-Munajjim), Muslim since about 818; head of the observations at Shammasiyya. Knows: Persian and Indian astronomy, the new observations behind the 'verified' tables (al-Zij al-Mumtahan). — Leads the Baghdad observations of 828–829. Dies in the caliph's train near Aleppo; the year is given as 830 or 832, so meet him early.
- **Sanad ibn Ali**: astronomer and instrument maker; built the observatory near the Shammasiyya gate. Knows: instruments (armillary, mural quadrant), observing, the arithmetic of tables. — A Jewish convert to Islam. Takes part in the observations at Baghdad and Damascus. Still alive in the 860s.
- **Khalid ibn Abd al-Malik al-Marwarrudhi**: astronomer, leads the observations on Mount Qasiyun at Damascus. Knows: solar and lunar observation. — Observes at Damascus in 831–833 while the caliph is in Syria; later sources name him in the degree measurement.
- **Ali ibn Isa al-Asturlabi**: maker of astrolabes and instruments. Knows: making and using astrolabes; writes a treatise on the astrolabe. — Named with Khalid in the measurement of a degree of the meridian. A craftsman who can build what a player draws in brass.
- **Habash al-Hasib al-Marwazi**: astronomer from Merv ('the calculator'). Knows: astronomical tables, the shadow functions (tangent and cotangent) in their early form, eclipse timing from star altitudes. — Observes for al-Ma'mun and lives on past 869, reportedly to a hundred.
- **al-Abbas ibn Said al-Jawhari**: geometer and astronomer. Knows: commentary on Euclid; attempts a proof of the parallel postulate. — Takes part in the Baghdad observations of 829–830 and the Damascus ones.
- **Abu Uthman al-Jahiz**: writer from Basra, Mu'tazilite, pupil of al-Nazzam. Knows: everything that interests him, animals, people, rhetoric, trades; observes ants, pigeons, and fish in his rich, rambling style. — Born c. 776, comes to Baghdad under al-Ma'mun, who admires his writing. His Book of Animals is written much later (c. 847). Dies 868/869.
- **Ibrahim ibn Sayyar al-Nazzam**: Mu'tazilite theologian and poet. Knows: denies Abu al-Hudhayl's atoms, holds that bodies are infinitely divisible and that motion crosses them by 'leaps'; sceptical of reports he cannot check. — In Baghdad. Dies some time between 836 and 845.
- **Abu al-Hudhayl al-Allaf**: elder of the Basra Mu'tazila. Knows: kalam atomism, indivisible parts and accidents; disputation. — Very old by 830; dies c. 841, reportedly near a hundred years old.
- **Bishr al-Marisi**: Hanafi jurist and theologian, the old champion of the created Quran. Knows: kalam and Hanafi law; was arguing the created Quran under Harun, decades before the caliph adopted it. — Born c. 755, hated by the traditionists. Dies in Baghdad in Rajab AH 218 (August 833), the summer the Mihna begins; some modern summaries give 813 in error.
- **Ahmad ibn Hanbal**: traditionist and jurist, the leading opponent of the created Quran. Knows: tens of thousands of prophetic reports, their chains of transmission. — Born 780, teaching in Baghdad. Refuses the Mihna in 833, is sent in chains toward the caliph, who dies before he arrives; flogged under al-Mu'tasim in 834 or 835 (sources differ) and released.
- **Ahmad ibn Abi Du'ad**: Mu'tazilite jurist and courtier. Knows: kalam, the case for the created Quran, the court. — Al-Ma'mun recommends him to his successor; under al-Mu'tasim he replaces Yahya ibn Aktham as chief judge (833–848) and runs the Mihna.
- **Yahya ibn Aktham**: chief judge (qadi al-qudat) and close companion of al-Ma'mun. Knows: law, the court. — Travels with the caliph. Replaced by Ibn Abi Du'ad on al-Mu'tasim's accession; chief judge again under al-Mutawakkil from 851.
- **Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Mus'abi**: Tahirid chief of police (sahib al-shurta) and in effect governor of Baghdad, c. 822–850. Knows: the city, its markets, prisons and quarters. — Executes the Mihna in Baghdad by the caliph's letters of 833. Guardian of the Banu Musa.
- **Abdallah ibn Tahir**: governor of Khurasan from 828. Knows: Khurasan, irrigation law (has jurists compile a book on qanat rights). — Rules from Nishapur; beyond reach except by letter or a long road.
- **Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi**: young hadith scholar from Balkh in Baghdad. Knows: traditions; despises the philosophers. — Born 787. Ibn al-Nadim says he turned to astrology at 47 after a quarrel with al-Kindi, which would be about 832–834. Becomes the most read astrologer of the Middle Ages.
- **Ishaq al-Mawsili**: court musician and boon companion. Knows: Arabic music theory and practice, the court's gossip. — Born 767; in favour with al-Ma'mun. Dies 850.
- **Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi**: the caliph's uncle, singer, briefly rival caliph (817–819). Knows: music, the Abbasid family. — Pardoned and living in Baghdad.
- **Giwargis II and Sabrisho II**: successive Catholicoi of the Church of the East, seated in Baghdad. Knows: the Nestorian church, its schools, physicians and scribes. — Giwargis holds office from 828 to about 830–831, Sabrisho from 831 to 835. The patriarch is the official head of the caliph's Christian subjects of this church.
- **Leo the Mathematician**: Byzantine scholar in Constantinople. Knows: Euclid and Greek mathematics, astronomy. — Elsewhere. A later Byzantine story has al-Ma'mun write to the emperor Theophilos asking for him; the date is doubtful and it may belong to al-Mu'tasim's reign.

## Events and timeline
- Each summer: the army leaves for the Byzantine frontier; Tigris and Euphrates floods in spring, low water and heat (well over 40 °C) from June to September.
- 827 (AH 212): al-Ma'mun publicly declares the Quran created and Ali the best of men after the Prophet.
- c. 827–828: Khalid ibn Abd al-Malik and Ali ibn Isa al-Asturlabi measure a degree of the meridian in the plain of Sinjar, about 56 2/3 Arabic miles (reports give 56 to 57; the date is not fixed).
- 828 (AH 213): solstice observations at the Shammasiyya quarter of Baghdad under Yahya ibn Abi Mansur; al-Khwarizmi is reported present. Abdallah ibn Tahir becomes governor of Khurasan.
- 829: Theophilos becomes Byzantine emperor. Observations at Shammasiyya continue into 829–830.
- 829/831–832 (start disputed): the Bashmurite revolt of Christian Copts in the Nile delta, crushed when the caliph comes to Egypt with al-Afshin.
- 830 (AH 215) spring–summer: al-Ma'mun leads his first personal campaign into Byzantine territory, the first by a caliph in twenty years, takes Majida by surrender and storms and razes Qurra (July 830); Sundus also falls. Yahya ibn Abi Mansur dies in his train near Aleppo (830, or 832).
- 831: second campaign; Heraclea Cybistra and Tyana surrender. Observations on Mount Qasiyun at Damascus begin.
- 831 10 Jul: Zubayda, Harun's widow and al-Amin's mother, dies in Baghdad.
- 832: the frontier fortress of Loulon falls after a long siege (date disputed); al-Ma'mun in Egypt to end the Bashmurite revolt.
- 833 spring (AH 218): from Raqqa and the frontier the caliph writes to Ishaq ibn Ibrahim in Baghdad: judges and traditionists must declare the Quran created or lose office. The Mihna begins. Ahmad ibn Hanbal refuses and is sent in chains to the caliph.
- 833 25 May: al-Abbas ibn al-Ma'mun crosses into Byzantine territory and begins building a fortress at Tyana.
- 833 7 Aug (some sources 9 Aug): al-Ma'mun dies of a fever on campaign near Tarsus and is buried there. Al-Mu'tasim is proclaimed, abandons the campaign and razes Tyana.
- 834 or 835: Ahmad ibn Hanbal is questioned before al-Mu'tasim, flogged and released. The Zutt of the southern marshes are defeated and deported (834/835). Babak's Khurramite revolt in Azerbaijan, going since 816, goes on until 837.
- 836: al-Mu'tasim moves court and Turkish army to the new city of Samarra.
- 848–851: al-Mutawakkil abandons the Mihna; Yahya ibn Aktham is chief judge again from 851.

## Quest hooks
- Al-Khwarizmi's new book solves inheritance shares by al-jabr; the clerks of the land-tax office still reckon on their fingers. Race one with the nine digits and zero, on paper, before the diwan.
- A copyist in the Suq al-Warraqin spends three months on a single Galen; show what carved wooden blocks and paper could do, and find out who would want a hundred identical copies of anything.
- The astronomers measuring a degree need a better instrument, and Sanad ibn Ali will build in brass what is drawn clearly enough.
- Ibn Masawayh has never tested one remedy against another: the bimaristan has the patients for a fair trial, if someone can explain why to compare.
- The perfumers distil rose water in alembics. Push the still further, to strong spirit, and decide what to tell anyone about burning wine.
- A glassmaker in Karkh grinds a clear lump; can it be made into a lens for an old scribe's failing eyes?
- The Mihna is coming in 833. A protector who swears the Quran is created may not protect for long; a traditionist who refuses may be flogged. The player knows both outcomes.
- Al-Ma'mun dies in August 833 of a fever after eating fresh dates and drinking cold water by a river (the chroniclers' story). The player could try to change what he eats and drinks, or not.
- The salt is rising in the southern fields of the Sawad. Explain drainage before it is too late for a village.
- A Basra merchant sailing for China wants a way to find his way when the stars are clouded.
- The Banu Musa are young, rich and bored. Give them a problem worth their money, an automaton, a pump, a clock that runs at night.
- Al-Kindi is collecting Greek books on mirrors: does light go out from the eye or come in to it?
- The caliph's brother is buying Turkish slave-soldiers. Military advice given to him decides the next half-century of the caliphate.
- A Byzantine prisoner from the frontier is a mathematician. Exchange, ransom or keep him?
- Gondeshapur still trains physicians: is there a cleaner way to run a ward? Washed hands, boiled water, separate rooms for fevers.
